lesson.section: 31. Cerebral Arteries and Circle of Willis

steps.title: Cerebral Arteries and Circle of Willis
steps.body: Brain arterial supply comes from internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems. The circle of Willis connects anterior and posterior circulations around the optic chiasm, infundibulum, and hypothalamic region.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Internal carotid gives anterior cerebral and middle cerebral arteries plus ophthalmic and communicating branches. Anterior cerebral arteries are connected by anterior communicating artery. Middle cerebral artery passes into lateral sulcus and supplies much of lateral hemisphere. Vertebral arteries form basilar artery; basilar divides into posterior cerebral arteries. Posterior communicating arteries connect internal carotid to posterior cerebral arteries.

steps.title: Why can an internal-capsule lesion affect several body regions at once?
steps.body: Projection fibers converge through a relatively compact white-matter corridor between deep nuclei. Damage to a small portion can therefore interrupt many descending or ascending pathways that were spread widely across the cortex. Deep perforating arteries supply this region, creating a vascular context different from a broad cortical branch territory. A small lesion volume does not imply a minor functional effect. To understand this, trace cortex-to-brainstem fibers through the capsule rather than considering only surface arterial maps.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: ACA mainly serves medial frontal and parietal surfaces, MCA much of the lateral hemisphere, and PCA occipital and inferior temporal territories. Deep perforators supply structures such as the internal capsule, so a small deep lesion can produce substantial deficits. The circle of Willis offers potential collateral connections, but variation and vessel caliber limit protection. MCA is a major branch leaving the circle, not one of the arteries forming its closed ring.
